title: Object Construction, Destruction and Slicing
objectives: Trace the exact construction and destruction sequence for objects with base subobjects and members
Identify when the copy constructor and copy assignment are invoked
Recognize object slicing, explain its cause, and prevent it with references, pointer containers or a deleted base copy
Keep invariants across all construction paths using delegating constructors and in-class defaults
motivation: Subtle PnL bugs hide in object lifetimes: a copy made in the wrong place reports yesterday state, and a derived position pushed into a base-valued container silently loses its option fields. C++ destroys objects deterministically - at scope exit, in reverse construction order - which is precisely what makes RAII possible. This lesson makes the construction and destruction sequence explicit, then attacks the classic value-semantics trap: object slicing.

blocks.md: An object lifetime begins when its constructor completes and ends when its destructor **starts**. For an object with a base class and members, construction follows a fixed recipe: direct base classes in declaration order (virtual bases, if any, first), then members in declaration order, then the constructor body. Destruction is the exact mirror image - derived destructor body first, then members in reverse, then the base. A delegating constructor behaves as its target constructor followed by a body, and in-class default initializers apply whenever the initializer list omits the member.

blocks.caption: Output 'cA cB dB cC dC dA': scope exit destroys in reverse creation order - B inside the block, then C, then A at the end of main.

blocks.md: The **copy constructor** fires when a new object is initialized from an existing one: `Order b = a;`, pass-by-value, and return-by-value (compilers routinely elide the last case - never count on observing it). The **copy assignment** fires when an already-existing object is assigned. Both are generated memberwise when you do not write them, and both must preserve the class invariant. Copies of large objects are real work, so hot paths pass heavy or polymorphic types by `const&` - which, unlike pass-by-value, also preserves the dynamic type.

blocks.caption: riskCheck takes Order by value: one copy appears, and both objects destroy in reverse order at scope exit.

blocks.md: Copying a Derived object into a Base **value** copies only the base subobject: the compiler selects the Base copy constructor from the static type at compile time. The derived members never arrive, and the vptr in the new object points at the Base vtable - so even virtual calls afterwards behave as Base. The code compiles and runs, which is what makes slicing dangerous: PnL reports go quietly wrong with no error anywhere.

blocks.caption: Same object, two parameter styles: the by-value copy slices, the reference dispatches.

blocks.title: Containers slice
blocks.md: `std::vector<Instrument>` stores values: push_back(option) constructs an Instrument from the Option - sliced, silently. Store pointers (std::vector<Instrument*>, or the smart pointers of the memory module), or delete the base copy constructor to turn slicing into a compile error.

Three defenses, in increasing strictness. Pass polymorphic types by reference or pointer. Store pointers in containers. And as a hard guarantee, make the base non-copyable - `Instrument(const Instrument&) = delete;` - so any by-value pass fails to compile. Value semantics belong to concrete types; a dynamic type needs indirection to survive.

segments: Instrument subobject (the only part a slice copies)

blocks.caption: Slicing copies only the base part of the object into the new one; the derived members and the derived vtable link never make it.

blocks.md: Every constructor is an entry point that must establish the invariant, so funnel the work: delegating constructors route through one primary validating constructor; in-class defaults such as `double realized_ = 0.0;` mean no constructor can forget a starting value; and the generated copy operations, copying memberwise, preserve invariants that depend only on member values. When a class manages a resource beyond plain members, copies need custom logic - the Rule of Three/Five lesson makes that systematic.

hints: auditByValue takes Instrument by value: only the base copy constructor participates in the slice.
Destruction is reverse construction order; the by-value parameter dies before auditByRef ever runs.
guidedExercise.solution:
Exact stdout:

```
ctor Instrument
ctor Option
copy Instrument
Instrument
dtor Instrument
Option
dtor Option
dtor Instrument
```

Line by line: constructing the Option builds the base subobject first (ctor Instrument), then the derived ctor body (ctor Option). auditByValue takes its parameter by value, so the Instrument copy constructor runs on the base subobject only (copy Instrument - no Option state travels, no Option ctor or dtor appears). Inside, the parameter is a genuine Instrument, so kind() dispatches to Instrument::kind(). At the end of the call the parameter is destroyed (dtor Instrument) - before auditByRef runs. auditByRef binds a reference: no copy, dynamic type intact, kind() dispatches to Option::kind(). At scope exit the Option is destroyed in reverse order: dtor Option, then its base subobject (dtor Instrument).

independentExercise.prompt: Define an abstract `Position` with a pure virtual `double pnl() const` and a virtual destructor. Derive `StockPosition` (fields qty, entry, last; pnl = qty x (last - entry)) and `OptionPosition` (same fields; pnl = qty x (last - entry) x 100.0 for the contract multiplier). Write `double bookPnl(const std::vector<Position*>&)` summing through the base pointers. Load StockPosition{100, 42.00, 42.50} and OptionPosition{-10, 3.20, 3.80}, print the total, and clean up with delete. Then answer: why can the container not be `std::vector<Position>`?
hints: Short positions carry a negative quantity; the sign handles direction.
Position is abstract - a value container would have to construct Position objects.

commonMistakes: Passing polymorphic types by value - slicing - and then reading the wrong virtual function result.
Using std::vector<Base> for heterogeneous collections instead of pointers.
Assuming the initializer-list order controls construction when declaration order does.
Expecting the copy constructor to run on every return statement - compilers elide copies.
Forgetting destruction is reverse construction order when reasoning about cleanup sequencing.
Adding a validating constructor but a second default constructor that skips the validation instead of delegating.
realWorldApplication: Trading systems rely on deterministic destruction to release locks, sockets and order state exactly at scope exit; a sliced position object inside a risk aggregator is a genuine production incident category.
quantFinanceApplication: Heterogeneous books are stored as base-class pointers and valued through virtual pnl()/pv() calls; slicing is precisely why a positions table typed as values reports every option as its underlying.
summary: Construction: base subobjects (declaration order), then members (declaration order), then the body; destruction is the exact reverse.
The copy constructor fires on initialization from an existing object (including pass-by-value); copy assignment fires on assignment to an existing object; both are memberwise by default.
Slicing: copying a Derived into a Base value copies only the base subobject and re-targets the vptr, so virtual calls act as Base.
Prevent slicing by passing references/pointers, storing pointers in containers, or deleting the base copy constructor.
Delegating constructors plus in-class default initializers give every construction path the same invariant.

quiz.answer: cA cB dB cC dC dA
quiz.explanation: A and B construct; the inner block ends and B is destroyed immediately (dB); C constructs; at the end of main, C is destroyed first, then A - destruction in reverse construction order.

bookAsValue takes Instrument by value, so the argument is copy-constructed from the base subobject only (slicing): the parameter is genuinely an Instrument and kind() reports Instrument. bookAsRef binds a reference, the dynamic type survives, and kind() dispatches to Option.

quiz.prompt: Why exactly does `Base b = derivedObj;` slice?
options: The Base copy constructor is selected from the static type at compile time, so only the Base subobject is copied
C++ deletes derived members during assignment
The vtable shrinks the object to fit
quiz.explanation: The target b has static type Base, so the compiler chooses Base(const Base&) and feeds it a Base& view of the derived object. The derived members and vtable link are simply never copied - it is compile-time selection, not a runtime decision.

quiz.prompt: Which are sound defenses against object slicing?
options: Pass polymorphic types by const reference
quiz.explanation: References and pointers preserve the dynamic type; pointer containers hold complete objects; deleting Base(const Base&) makes any by-value pass a compile error. Access specifiers on derived members do nothing about base-value copies.

quiz.prompt: An OptionPosition holds qty -10, entry 3.20, last 3.80, and computes pnl() = qty x (last - entry) x 100. What is its pnl?
quiz.explanation: $-10 \times 0.60 \times 100 = -600$: a short option position that moved against the desk. Slicing this object into a Position value would lose the x100 multiplier entirely.

quiz.prompt: In one or two sentences: why does deterministic destruction matter in trading systems?
quiz.modelAnswer: Objects release resources (locks, sockets, orders) at a known instant - scope exit, in reverse order - which enables RAII; unpredictable GC-style cleanup would break latency budgets and correctness.
quiz.explanation: C++ ties destruction to scope exit in reverse construction order, so resource release timing is exact and compiler-enforced - the foundation of RAII, and the reason latency-critical desks avoid garbage collection.

flashcards.back: Construct: bases in declaration order, members in declaration order, body. Destroy: derived body, members reversed, base - the exact reverse.

flashcards.front: Trade prints "cX" on construction and "dX" on destruction. main: Trade a{"A"}; { Trade b{"B"}; } Trade c{"C"}; - what prints?
flashcards.back: cA cB dB cC dC dA - inner scopes destroy immediately; main destroys in reverse creation order.

Copying a Derived object into a Base value copies only the base subobject (chosen from the static type at compile time); derived state and the derived vtable link are lost, so virtual calls act as Base.

flashcards.front: void audit(Instrument inst); audit(option); reports kind() == "Instrument" for an Option. Fix?
flashcards.back: Take the parameter as const Instrument& (or a pointer). By-value parameters slice; references preserve the dynamic type.

flashcards.front: Copy constructor vs copy assignment - when does each fire?
flashcards.back: Copy ctor: a NEW object is initialized from an existing one (T b = a; pass-by-value; return-by-value pre-elision). Assignment: an EXISTING object is assigned (b = a;).
